thread.title: Fed Chair Powell Faces Rate Hike Rebellion as Bond Traders Bet on 2020 Cuts

author: Martin Baccardax
title: Fed Chair Powell Faces Rate Hike Rebellion as Bond Traders Bet on 2020 Cuts
text:
U.S. interest rate traders have made their strongest challenge to date against the Federal Reserve's signalling of two more hikes in 2019, with investors now betting on a near-term cut in the benchmark rate following sharp slowdown in manufacturing activity in the world's two biggest economies.
The shift in sentiment comes just hours before a crucial December jobs report that could either cement or alter the Fed's positioning on rates, which it sees rising "gradually" this year as the economy improves, and speech from Chairman Jerome Powell later today in Atlanta. It also follows a troubling warning on revenue from Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) and persistent declines in U.S. stocks that have tipped the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite index into bear market territory.
"Financial markets are clearly nervous about the US' economic prospects with the government shutdown and clear disagreements between the President and the Federal Reserve on policy direction adding to the unease," said ING's chief international economist James Knightley. "However, business surveys remain in decent shape with any slowdown in jobs growth more due to a lack of available workers than any cut backs to business expansion plans - at this stage."
The CME Group's FedWatch tool, which assigns rate hike probabilities based on futures trading, is now suggesting a 39.2% chance of a reduction in the Fed Funds in January 2020, as well as a 35% chance of cut in December 2019. Alongside that shift, benchmark 2-year Treasury note yields slipped to 2.37% last night, trading below the top end of the Fed Funds rate of 2.5% for the first time since 2008.
US 2y yield has collapsed to 2.37% as the global slowdown is headline news in the US, essentially saying the Fed is done. US 2yr yield is now 60 bps off its high water mark of less than 2mths ago. Trade below Fed Funds rate, so mkts expects rate cuts within next 2yrs. (via RTRS) pic.twitter.com/4iMTSm8DyD
— Holger Zschaepitz (@Schuldensuehner) January 3, 2019 Bond yields have in fact fallen sharply this week after a key reading of manufacturing activity for the month of December notched its biggest decline in a decade, following on from weaker factory data in major economies around the world.
The ISM Manufacturing Activity index fell to 54.1 points in December, well above the 50 mark that separate growth from contraction but well shy of the 59.3 tally in November and the 57.9 Street consensus. The index is now at the lowest since November 2016, led to the downside by an 11-point slump in new orders to 51.1 from 62.1 and a 2-point slide in employment activity, to 56.2 from 58.4.
"Growth appears to have stopped," one of the ISM respondents commented. "Resources still focused on re-sourcing for U.S. tariff mitigation out of China."
The U.S. data followed a key private reading of manufacturing activity in China on Wednesday, the Caixin-Markit PMI, showing a slip the 50 level for the first time in 19 months, according to data published Wednesday, as similar activity gauges around the region showed associated weakness over the month of December.
Europe's key manufacturing sector also closed out 2018 on a weak note, with the IHS Markit assessment published Wednesday sliding to the lowest level since February 2016 and activity in Germany slipping to a 33-month low.
"That makes Powell's comments today all the more interesting, as he appears alongside his predecessors Janet Yellen and Ben Bernanke for a panel discussion," said Craig Erlam, senior market analyst at Oanda. "I doubt Powell will use this platform to announce any significant shift in Fed policy but he may address the sizeable difference between central bank and market expectations for the coming year."
This week's market moves, particularly in foreign exchange markets, where the yen surged more than 4% against the U.S. dollar in a matter of minutes yesterday -- an ominous 'risk-off' spike that echoed previous moves prior to both the Russian debt crisis in 1998 and the global financial crisis ten years later -- have dislocated markets to the point where interest rate futures may be too far ahead of the underling fundamentals.
Manufacturing makes up only 12% of GDP and less than 9% of payrolls additions, argues Ian Shepherdson of Pantheon Economics, how thinks the continued strength of the consumer, which fuels more than two thirds of U.S. GDP, will support December jobs growth, "maintaining the downward trend in unemployment."
"We'd be surprised to see a tightening before June-we're pondering moving our forecast to September-but the bar for the Fed to ease is much higher than markets want to believe, especially if we're right about a trade deal," he said.
